name: Amira Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Piotr and I run a small family building firm, nine of us including our son-in-law Marek, who's the site manager now. We do custom houses and big extensions, people who want oak frames and glass and something nobody else has. I'm still the lead carpenter, so most mornings I'm on site with the crew by seven, and evenings I'm at the kitchen table doing estimates. This week it's a timber-frame house on a steep plot by the river, which is a puzzle I love.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the client's face at handover, when it's exactly what they drew on a napkin two years earlier. And I enjoy that it's ours, the family name on the van. What wears me out is the hours, and the big national builders undercutting us on price, they can buy timber in bulk we can't.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I fly a drone over each plot and the AI turns it into a 3D model, so I can show clients their house on the actual slope before we dig. I use the chat ones to draft estimates and check building rules, and I've got an app that tracks timber prices. Piotr calls me the robot lady, but he's quite happy when the estimates are done in an hour instead of a weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the small firms can keep doing what we do best. At church, people would ask me since I'm the one with the drone, and I'd say it's a tool, not a miracle. Online I'd post a picture of an oak frame and say no app built this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing changes. We've got savings, the house is paid off, and the firm's doing well. I'd keep using the tools I like and plan to hand the firm over to Kasia and Marek in about five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Maybe buy a better drone and a newer modelling program, a couple of thousand. And take on another apprentice, because there's work, and young people need a start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit disappointed, I like new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would the apprentice be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a girl called Ewa, from the church youth group, she's been helping on Saturdays. She's fierce with a tape measure. I'd want her to learn the old joints and the drone, both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about this picture bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that the big builders would carry on undercutting us. If the tools don't get better, we can't get faster to compete. But we've managed this long on quality, we'd manage.

S0.say: Good, small firms can keep doing what they do best, and AI is a tool, not a miracle. Online she'd post an oak frame and say no app built it.
S0.think: Nothing changes for her, with savings, a paid-off house and a healthy firm she plans to hand to her daughter and son-in-law in about five years.
S0.do: Keeps going and spends a couple of thousand on a better drone and modelling program. Takes on another apprentice from the church youth group.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly disappointed, because she likes new things.
S0.quote: Online I'd post a picture of an oak frame and say no app built this.
S0.fieldNote: Amira is a family-firm owner who loves technology and traditional values in equal measure. She'd be disappointed if AI stayed small because better tools are how her firm competes with big builders. Her succession plan to her daughter and son-in-law runs through everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for small firms to punch above their weight. At church I'd say learn the tools, work hard, and you'll be fine. I'd post about how we use them, because I'm proud of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for us. Custom work is hard to automate, but the planning, estimating and ordering can all be faster. We could take on more jobs without hiring an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, I'd look at a robot for cutting the oak joints in the yard, the kind that reads a 3D model, maybe forty or fifty thousand. I'd send Marek on courses for the new planning tools. And I'd keep training apprentices, but on both the old and new ways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, excited really. Like getting a new set of tools for Christmas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fifty thousand is a big step for a nine-person firm. How would you decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run the numbers with Piotr and Marek over a weekend. If it pays for itself in three years, we do it. I'd rather borrow for a machine that makes us faster than sit and watch the big builders get there first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the firm would find it hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Piotr, a bit. He's a hand joiner, he loves his chisels. I'd make sure the robot does the rough cutting and he does the fine work, the bits clients see. He'd grumble but he'd come round.

S1.say: This is a chance for small firms to punch above their weight: learn the tools, work hard and you'll be fine. She'd post proudly about how her firm uses them.
S1.think: It's good for her firm, because custom work is hard to automate but planning, estimating and ordering can all speed up, letting them take more jobs without hiring an office.
S1.do: Looks at a forty to fifty thousand robot for cutting oak joints in the yard, deciding with her husband and son-in-law whether it pays back in three years. Sends her son-in-law on planning courses and trains apprentices in both old and new ways.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, like getting new tools for Christmas.
S1.quote: I'd rather borrow for a machine that makes us faster than sit and watch the big builders get there first.
S1.fieldNote: Amira sees steady change as a competitive edge for her small firm against national builders. She'd borrow and invest decisively, with a three-year payback test. She plans to keep her husband on the fine hand work, balancing family and machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one moves much faster. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be a shock, and families need to stick together. At church I'd say we need to look after each other, and the young people especially. I'd still say learn the tools, but I'd admit it's going to be hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, I'd be sixty and I'd be fine. But the firm worries me. If the big builders get robots that can do anything in two years, they'll be faster and cheaper than us, and the firm I was handing to Kasia and Marek could be gone before they've had it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd buy whatever robots we could afford, quickly, so we're not left behind. I'd sit down with Kasia and Marek and talk about handing over the firm now, not in five years, so they can steer it while I'm still here to help. And I'd keep some savings back, in case the firm needs a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited by the tools, worried for the family business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider selling up instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if someone offered a good price, but I don't think anyone would buy a small firm in that mess. And it's our name, I'd rather fight for it. Kasia grew up in that yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your apprentices, like Ewa?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to learn the robots and learn the joints, both, and to never think she's too good for any job. And that if it comes to it, she can always build for her own family and neighbours. That never goes away.

S2.say: It'll be a shock and families need to stick together, looking after young people especially. She'd still say learn the tools but admit it will be hard.
S2.think: She'd be fine personally at sixty, but big builders with robots could undercut her firm and the business she was handing to her daughter and son-in-law could be gone before they've had it.
S2.do: Buys whatever robots the firm can afford, quickly, and hands the firm to her daughter and son-in-law now instead of in five years while she can still help. Keeps some savings back as a cushion for the business.
S2.feel: Uneasy, excited by the tools but worried for the family business.
S2.quote: Kasia grew up in that yard.
S2.fieldNote: The fast case threatens Amira's legacy rather than her own finances. Her instinct is to move faster, buying robots and bringing the handover forward. She rejects selling because of what the firm means to her family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, with five years. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for a small firm to get ready if it's smart. At church I'd say prepare, learn, help each other. I'd post about how we're getting ready, to encourage other small builders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's a good amount of time. I'd be sixty-three, and I could hand the firm over properly with the new tools in place. Kasia and Marek would have time to learn to run a firm with robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd invest in the joint-cutting robot in the first year, and add more as they come. I'd plan the handover for about three years from now, with me staying on part time. And I'd keep training apprentices, so the next generation knows the craft and the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Kasia and Marek to keep from the old way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Meeting the client on the plot, standing there together. A robot can draw a house, but someone has to listen to what people actually want. That's the bit I'd want them to never hand over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about the big builders differently with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, they'll do what they do, and that's fair, it's a free market. Our job is to be better at what they can't do. I'd rather compete than complain.

S3.say: Five years is enough for a smart small firm to get ready: prepare, learn and help each other. She'd post about her firm's preparations to encourage other small builders.
S3.think: Five years suits her: at sixty-three she could hand the firm over properly with new tools in place, giving her daughter and son-in-law time to learn to run it with robots.
S3.do: Invests in the joint-cutting robot in the first year and adds more as they come. Plans the handover for about three years out while staying part time, and keeps training apprentices in craft and machines.
S3.feel: Calm, as if she has a plan.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Amira turns the threat into a structured handover plan. She accepts big builders' advantages as a fair free market and wants to win on what they can't do. Meeting clients on the plot is the human core she wants kept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to learn. At church I'd say prepare and trust God. I'd tell the young ones to learn a trade and the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's easy. I'd be sixty-eight, retired, the firm in Kasia and Marek's hands. They'd have a decade to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand over the firm in about five years, as I'd planned, once the new tools are working. Then I'd step back, maybe help out with the drone surveys now and then. And I'd keep some money in the business, as a silent partner, to help them buy the machines they need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Looking forward to seeing what they do with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you most like to see the firm doing in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still building oak houses people love, but with half the backache. Robots lifting the beams, Marek on the tablet, and somebody young cutting the last joint by hand because the client wants to see it done. That would make me happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that the young ones won't get the hard years that taught me. I learned by carrying timber and getting shouted at. I don't want them soft, but I don't want them broken either.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty for anyone willing to learn, so prepare and trust God. She'd tell young people to learn a trade and the machines.
S4.think: At sixty-eight she'd be retired with the firm in her daughter and son-in-law's hands, and they'd have a decade to get ready.
S4.do: Hands over the firm in about five years as planned, once the new tools are working, and steps back to help with drone surveys now and then. Keeps money in the business as a silent partner to help buy machines.
S4.feel: Calm and looking forward to what the next generation does.
S4.quote: Robots lifting the beams, Marek on the tablet, and somebody young cutting the last joint by hand because the client wants to see it done.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Amira is calm and focused on legacy, picturing a blend of robots and hand craft. She plans to stay invested as a silent partner. Her one worry is that young workers might miss the hard years that shaped her.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it could take the firm before Kasia and Marek have had a chance. What would help is fair access to the new machines for small firms, maybe through loans or leasing, and apprenticeships that keep going, so young people still learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what clients want. Most of my clients aren't paying for a house, they're paying for a story they can tell, that it was built by a family firm that cared. I don't think that goes away, even with robots.

headlineQuote: Most of my clients aren't paying for a house, they're paying for a story they can tell, that it was built by a family firm that cared.
portrait: Amira Kowalski is a 58-year-old lead carpenter who runs a small family building firm with her husband, making custom oak-frame houses, and plans to hand it to her daughter and son-in-law. She uses AI every day, from drone surveys to estimates, and sees the tools as how a small firm competes with national builders. She believes in a free market, faith and apprenticeships, and would rather compete than complain. The two-year AGI picture leaves her uneasy, worried that big builders with robots could sink the firm before her family inherits it, so she'd buy robots and bring the handover forward. With more time she calmly plans a handover with the new tools in place.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI scenario, because it could take the family firm before her daughter and son-in-law have a chance to run it.
whatWouldHelp: Fair access to new machines for small firms through loans or leasing, and apprenticeships that keep going so young people still learn.
